cards.title: ISMP: don't write these
cards.body: Some abbreviations cause real errors. **QD** (daily) gets misread as QID; **QOD** as QD; **U** for units looks like 0 or 4; **IU** looks like IV or 10; **trailing zeros** (5.0 mg → read as 50 mg) and **naked decimals** (.5 mg → 5 mg). Write “daily”, “units”, and 0.5 mg.
cards.source: ISMP List of Error-Prone Abbreviations; Joint Commission Do Not Use List

cards.title: Eyes vs. ears
cards.body: **OD** right eye · **OS** left eye · **OU** both eyes. **AD** right ear · **AS** left ear · **AU** both ears. ISMP lists all six as error-prone (eye/ear mix-ups!), so many pharmacies now spell them out.

cards.title: Decode a sig
steps: Read the Rx: “Amoxicillin 500 mg cap. Sig: 1 cap po tid x 10 d. Disp #30”
“1 cap” → take one capsule
“po” → by mouth
“tid” → three times a day
“x 10 d” → for 10 days
Check the math: 1 × 3 × 10 = 30 ✔ matches Disp #30
Label: “Take 1 capsule by mouth three times a day for 10 days.”

cards.title: DEA schedule
cards.back: High abuse potential, no currently accepted medical use in the US (e.g., heroin, LSD).

cards.title: Days supply, step by step
steps: Rx: Metformin 500 mg, 1 tab po bid, #180
Doses per day: bid = 2
Tablets per day: 1 × 2 = 2
Days supply = quantity ÷ per day

cards.title: Counting tablets on a tray
steps: Verify the drug, strength & NDC match the Rx
Pour tablets onto a clean counting tray
Use the spatula to slide them in groups of 5
Count 5, 10, 15… to the Rx quantity
Slide the counted tablets into the chute & return extras to stock bottle
Close the stock bottle right away (prevents mix-ups)
Pharmacist does final verification

cards.title: Early refill
cards.setup: A patient wants to refill their oxycodone/APAP (C-II) prescription. You look it up: it was filled 12 days ago for a 30-day supply. What do you do?

choices.text: Refill it — they have a valid Rx
choices.result: C-II prescriptions can't be refilled, and this would also be very early. ❌

choices.text: Tell them politely you'll need the pharmacist, and alert the pharmacist
choices.result: Right. Controlled-substance and early-fill decisions go to the pharmacist. ✅

choices.text: Give them a few tablets from stock to tide them over
choices.result: Never. That's dispensing without a valid Rx — a serious violation. ❌

cards.title: Look-alike, sound-alike
cards.setup: The Rx says hydroxyzine 25 mg. On the shelf, hydralazine 25 mg sits right next to it. The bottle you grabbed says “hydra…”. What now?

choices.result: Hydralazine is a BP drug; hydroxyzine is an antihistamine. Classic LASA error. ❌

choices.text: Stop, compare the full name and NDC to the Rx, and grab the correct bottle
choices.result: Yes — always match name, strength, dosage form AND NDC. ✅

cards.source: ISMP List of Confused Drug Names

cards.title: What the NDC tells you
cards.body: The **National Drug Code** is a 10-digit, 3-segment number (labeler – product – package), often shown as 11 digits for billing (5-4-2). Scanning it during fill catches wrong-drug errors.

cards.title: Hear it: the 5 rights
cards.text: The five rights of medication administration are: the right patient, the right drug, the right dose, the right route, and the right time.

cards.title: Say it out loud

cards.title: 3 kinds of health information exchange
cards.body: **Directed** exchange: sending info provider-to-provider (like secure email). **Query-based**: searching for a patient's info, e.g. in the ER. **Consumer-mediated**: the patient collects and shares their own data.

cards.title: Meaningful Use → Promoting Interoperability
cards.body: HITECH (2009) paid providers to adopt **certified EHR technology** and use it meaningfully: Stage 1 data capture, Stage 2 advanced clinical processes, Stage 3 improved outcomes. In 2018 CMS renamed it **Promoting Interoperability**.

cards.title: Hear it: SOAP
cards.text: A SOAP note has four parts. Subjective: what the patient tells you. Objective: what you measure, like vital signs. Assessment: the diagnosis or impression. Plan: what happens next.

cards.title: Hear it: code sets
cards.text: ICD ten CM tells why the patient was seen. CPT tells what was done. HCPCS level two covers supplies and equipment. Together they tell the payer the whole story.

cards.title: Say it out loud
cards.prompt: What do the letters in SOAP stand for?

cards.title: Say it out loud
cards.prompt: Which code set is used for diagnoses?

cards.title: Register a new patient in the EHR
steps: Search the MPI first (name + DOB) — avoid duplicates
Not found → create new record
Enter demographics: legal name, DOB, sex, address, phone
Scan photo ID and insurance card (front & back)
Run an eligibility check (270/271)
Get signed HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgment
Save → patient ready for scheduling

cards.title: Life of a claim
steps: Visit documented in EHR
Coder assigns ICD-10-CM + CPT/HCPCS
Charges entered; claim built (837P)
Claim scrubber checks for errors
Sent through clearinghouse to payer
Payer adjudicates: pay, deny, or reject
835 remittance posted; patient billed for balance

cards.title: Wrong chart
cards.setup: You're documenting vitals and realize you opened the chart of a different patient with the same last name. You've already saved the BP.

choices.text: Delete the entry so nobody sees it
choices.result: Never delete. EHR changes must be traceable. ❌

choices.text: Follow the correction process: mark the entry as entered in error with your reason, then document in the right chart
choices.result: Correct — the audit trail keeps the original plus the correction. ✅

choices.text: Leave it; it's just one BP
choices.result: Wrong data in a chart can harm the patient. ❌

cards.title: Phishing at the front desk
cards.setup: An email ‘from IT’ asks you to confirm your EHR password via a link before 5 PM or be locked out.

choices.text: Click and log in — don't want to be locked out
choices.result: That's how credentials and ePHI get stolen. ❌

choices.text: Don't click; report it to IT/security through a known channel
choices.result: Yes. Real IT never asks for your password by email. ✅

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: Under HIPAA, which disclosure does NOT need patient authorization?
choices: Telling a reporter about a celebrity patient
Posting a patient's photo on social media
Sharing with another provider for treatment
cards.explain: Treatment, Payment and Operations (TPO) are permitted without authorization.

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: A breach affects 600 people in one state. Who must be notified?
choices: Nobody if it was an accident
Individuals, HHS, and prominent media — within 60 days of discovery
cards.explain: 500+ residents of a state → media too; HHS within 60 days.

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: The ‘minimum necessary’ standard means…
choices: Store as little data as possible
Use/disclose only the least PHI needed for the purpose
cards.explain: Note: minimum necessary does NOT apply to disclosures to providers for treatment.

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: Who enforces HIPAA Privacy & Security Rules?
cards.explain: OCR investigates complaints and issues penalties.

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: Patients generally must get access to their records within…
choices: They have no right of access

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: HMO plans usually require…
choices: paying full price for primary care
a primary care provider and referrals to specialists
cards.explain: PPOs usually don't require referrals and cover some out-of-network care.

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: Who generally qualifies for Medicare?
choices: People 65+, some younger people with disabilities, and people with ESRD

cards.title: HIPAA & insurance
cards.question: A claim rejected for a missing field vs. denied by the payer — difference?
choices: Rejected = never processed (fix & resend); denied = processed but not paid (appeal)
cards.explain: Know the difference for revenue cycle questions.

cards.title: HIPAA in 3 rules
cards.body: **Privacy Rule**: who can see/share PHI. **Security Rule**: protecting *electronic* PHI with administrative, physical and technical safeguards. **Breach Notification Rule**: who to tell, and how fast, when PHI is exposed.

cards.title: 18 identifiers
cards.body: Safe-harbor de-identification removes **18 identifiers** — names, small geographic areas, dates (except year), phone, fax, email, SSN, MRN, plan numbers, account numbers, license numbers, vehicle IDs, device IDs, URLs, IP addresses, biometrics, full-face photos, and any other unique number or code.

cards.title: The revenue cycle
cards.body: Scheduling → **registration & eligibility** → visit & documentation → **coding** → charge entry → **claim submission** → payment posting → **denial management** → patient billing & collections. Every front-desk mistake shows up later as a denial.

cards.title: Hear it: SBAR handoff
cards.text: SBAR is a handoff format. Situation: what is happening now. Background: the relevant history. Assessment: what you think the problem is. Recommendation: what you need or suggest next.

cards.title: Hear it: TPO
cards.text: Under HIPAA, protected health information can be used without the patient's written authorization for treatment, payment, and health care operations. That's called T P O.

cards.title: Say it out loud
cards.prompt: What are the three types of HIPAA Security Rule safeguards?

cards.title: SBAR handoff, live
steps: S – “Mr. Lee, room 4, is short of breath since 2 PM.”
B – “68, COPD, admitted yesterday for pneumonia.”
A – “O2 sat dropped from 95% to 89%. I think he's getting worse.”
R – “Please come assess him now; should I start the ordered O2?”
Receiver reads back the key points ✔

cards.title: Verify insurance before a visit
steps: Collect card: member ID, group #, payer phone
Run eligibility (270/271) or payer portal
Confirm active coverage on the date of service
Note copay, deductible remaining, coinsurance
Check if referral / prior authorization is needed
Document everything in the account

cards.title: The curious neighbor
cards.setup: At the pharmacy counter, your neighbor says: “I saw Maria from our street here yesterday — what's she taking?”

choices.text: “Just her blood pressure pills, nothing serious.”
choices.result: That's a HIPAA violation — disclosing PHI with no permitted purpose. ❌

choices.text: “I'm sorry, I can't share anything about other customers. Can I help you with anything?”
choices.result: Perfect: friendly, no confirmation she was even a patient. ✅

choices.text: “I can't say, but it's for her heart.”

cards.title: Patient handoff
cards.setup: End of shift. You're handing off to the next tech: a pending prior auth for a patient's Ozempic is waiting on the doctor's office.

choices.text: “There's some PA thing, check the queue.”
“Patient X: semaglutide PA pending. Faxed Dr. Y at 2 PM. Insurer needs A1c. Call office by 10 AM; patient expects a call.”
choices.result: Clear SBAR-style handoff with who, what, status and next step. ✅

cards.title: Self-pay or bill it?
cards.setup: A patient says: “I'll pay cash for this visit — please don't send anything to my insurance.”

choices.text: Bill insurance anyway — rules are rules
choices.result: Under HIPAA, if a patient pays in full out of pocket, they can restrict disclosure to their health plan. ❌

choices.text: Honor it: collect payment in full and flag the restriction in the record
